Content:
We need to recognize when a particular series looks like a standard Maclaurin series. A list of some common Maclaurin series is given below.

Content:
[MATH: (1)/(1 − x) = 1 + x + x^{2} + ⋯ + x^{n} + ⋯ = ∑_(n = 0)^(∞)x^{n},|x ∈ (− 1, 1); (1)/(1 + x) = 1 − x + x^{2} − ⋯ + (− 1)^{n}x^{n} + ⋯ = ∑_(n = 0)^(∞)(− 1)^{n}x^{n},|x ∈ (− 1, 1); e^{x} = 1 + x + (1)/(2!)x^{2} + ⋯ + (x^{n})/(n!) + ⋯ = ∑_(n = 0)^(∞)(x^{n})/(n!),|x ∈ (− ∞, ∞); \ln (1 + x) = x − (1)/(2)x^{2} + (1)/(3)x^{3} − ⋯ + ((− 1)^{n + 1}x^{n})/(n) + ⋯ = ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)((− 1)^{n + 1}x^{n})/(n),|x ∈ (− 1, 1]; \sin (x) = x − (1)/(3!)x^{3} + (1)/(5!)x^{5} + ⋯ + ((− 1)^{n}x^{2n + 1})/((2n + 1)!) + ⋯ = ∑_(n = 0)^(∞)((− 1)^{n}x^{2n + 1})/((2n + 1)!),|x ∈ (− ∞, ∞); \cos (x) = 1 − (1)/(2!)x^{2} + (1)/(4!)x^{4} − ⋯ + ((− 1)^{n}x^{2n})/((2n)!) + ⋯ = ∑_(n = 0)^(∞)((− 1)^{n}x^{2n})/((2n)!),|x ∈ (− ∞, ∞)]

Content:
In this lesson, we will focus on recognizing the standard Maclaurin series for the geometric series, the exponential function, and the natural logarithm

sections.normalized_html:
The first thing we notice is that we can rewrite the terms of the series as powers of [MATH: \dfrac{2}{3}\mathbin{:}] [MATH: 1 + (2)/(3) + (4)/(9) + (8)/(27) + ⋯ + (2^{n})/(3^{n}) + ⋯|= 1 + (2)/(3) + (2^{2})/(3^{2}) + (2^{3})/(3^{3}) + ⋯ + (2^{n})/(3^{n}) + ⋯; = 1 + (2)/(3) + ((2)/(3))^{2} + ((2)/(3))^{3} + ⋯ + ((2)/(3))^{n} + ⋯]

Then, we recognize that the series looks similar to the Maclaurin expansion for [MATH: f({\color{blue}x}) = \dfrac{1}{1-{\color{blue}x}}.]

[MATH: (1)/(1 − x)|= 1 + x + x^{2} + x^{3} + ⋯ + x^{n} + ⋯]

Substituting [MATH: x={\color{blue}\dfrac{2}{3}}] into our Maclaurin expansion gives

[MATH: (1)/((1 − (2)/(3)))|= 1 + (2)/(3) + ((2)/(3))^{2} + ((2)/(3))^{3} + ⋯ + ((2)/(3))^{n} + ⋯; 3|= 1 + (2)/(3) + (4)/(9) + (8)/(27) + ⋯ + (2^{n})/(3^{n}) + ⋯.]

Therefore, the sum of the series is [MATH: 3.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The first thing we notice is that we can rewrite the terms of the series as powers of [MATH: \dfrac{2}{3}\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: 1 + (2)/(3) + (4)/(9) + (8)/(27) + ⋯ + (2^{n})/(3^{n}) + ⋯|= 1 + (2)/(3) + (2^{2})/(3^{2}) + (2^{3})/(3^{3}) + ⋯ + (2^{n})/(3^{n}) + ⋯; = 1 + (2)/(3) + ((2)/(3))^{2} + ((2)/(3))^{3} + ⋯ + ((2)/(3))^{n} + ⋯]

Then, we recognize that the series looks similar to the Maclaurin expansion for [MATH: f({\color{blue}x}) = \dfrac{1}{1-{\color{blue}x}}.]

[MATH: (1)/(1 − x)|= 1 + x + x^{2} + x^{3} + ⋯ + x^{n} + ⋯]

Substituting [MATH: x={\color{blue}\dfrac{2}{3}}] into our Maclaurin expansion gives

[MATH: (1)/((1 − (2)/(3)))|= 1 + (2)/(3) + ((2)/(3))^{2} + ((2)/(3))^{3} + ⋯ + ((2)/(3))^{n} + ⋯; 3|= 1 + (2)/(3) + (4)/(9) + (8)/(27) + ⋯ + (2^{n})/(3^{n}) + ⋯.]

Therefore, the sum of the series is [MATH: 3.]
